In quibus verbis insinuatur, quod cœlo et terra creatis, abyssus et aqua pariter exstiterunt, de quorum creatione non videbatur aliquid tangi in verbis his, In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram. Rursus paulo post legitur, firmamentum quod vocatum est cœlum, esse factum secunda die: idcirco obscurum fit de quo cœlo dicatur, In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram.
paras.en: These things premised, we must touch on the more celebrated expositions of what is said, [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]], as to this last little part, namely [[1:1|heaven, and earth|cœlum et terram]], and also as to the text that follows, the understanding of which depends in great part on the understanding and exposition of this part. Now this statement, [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]], taken by itself, does not seem hard to understand; but the words of the text that follow straight after bring in its difficulty. For straightway is added: [[1:2|darkness was upon the face of the deep; and the spirit of God moved over the waters|Tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi, et Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas]]. In these words it is implied that when heaven and earth had been created, the deep and the water existed as well, of whose creation nothing seemed to be touched on in these words, [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]]. Again, a little after we read that the firmament, which was called heaven, was made on the second day; and so it becomes obscure of which heaven it is said: [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]].

paras.t: Sanctus igitur Augustinus, considerans quod littera Genesis, quantum ad superficiem suam, patet irrisioni calumniisque infidelium, et eos a conversione ad fidem avertere potest, eo quod videatur instar poetarum et quorumdam philosophorum ab Aristotele satis reprobatorum, ponere quoddam chaos confusum in exordio mundi, excogitavit quamdam expositionem subtilem, per quam defendit Scripturam ab irrisione hujusmodi, et tamen salvavit Scripturæ ac fidei veritatem. Itaque dixit, quod sicut Deus omnipotens omnia in seipso unico actu intelligendi perfecte et distincte concipit et cognoscit, ac intra se exprimit, sic in eodem instanti omnia opera sex dierum simul et distincte produxit, eadem practice intelligendo atque ut essent jubendo. Cui expositioni videtur consonare illud in Psalmo: Ipse dixit, et facta sunt: ipse mandavit, et creata sunt. Et quod in Ecclesiastico legitur: Qui vivit in æternum, creavit omnia simul. Quod item Moyses ait: Dei perfecta sunt opera. Et quod in hoc ipso Genesis libro paulo post subditur: Istæ sunt generationes cœli et terræ, in die qua creavit Dominus cœlum et terram, et omne virgultum agri, omnemque herbam regionis, quum tamen virgulta et herbæ infra legantur tertia die producta.
paras.en: Holy Augustine, then, considering that the letter of Genesis, as to its surface, lies open to the mockery and calumnies of unbelievers and can turn them away from conversion to the faith, because, like the poets and certain philosophers well enough refuted by Aristotle, it seems to posit a kind of confused chaos at the beginning of the world, devised a subtle exposition by which he defended Scripture from mockery of this kind and yet kept safe the truth of Scripture and of the faith. And so he said that just as almighty God conceives and knows all things perfectly and distinctly in himself by a single act of understanding, and expresses them within himself, so in the same instant he produced all the works of the six days together and distinctly, understanding them practically [that is, with the knowledge that makes, not merely the knowledge that beholds] and commanding that they be. With this exposition that in the Psalm seems to agree: [[Ps 32:9|he spoke and they were made: he commanded and they were created|Ipse dixit, et facta sunt: ipse mandavit, et creata sunt]]. And what is read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 18:1|He that liveth for ever created all things together|Qui vivit in æternum, creavit omnia simul]]. And what Moses likewise says: [[Deut 32:4|The works of God are perfect|Dei perfecta sunt opera]]. And what is added a little after in this very book of Genesis: [[Gen 2:4|These are the generations of the heaven and the earth|Istæ sunt generationes cœli et terræ]], [[Gen 2:4|in the day that the Lord God made the heaven and the earth|in die qua creavit Dominus cœlum et terram]], [[Gen 2:5|and every plant of the field|et omne virgultum agri]], [[Gen 2:5|and every herb of the ground|omnemque herbam regionis]] [the margin gives Gen. ii, 5 only; the quotation begins in 2:4], whereas the plants and herbs are read further on to have been brought forth on the third day.

paras.t: Hæc ergo intuens Augustinus, dicit opera sex dierum simul facta distincte. Unde ait Albertus libro de Coæquævis: Augustinus revera ponit omnia simul creata in materia et forma, quæ scilicet natura non potest per se producere motu superiorum, videlicet cœlestium corporum et commixtione elementorum. Et ideo cœlum a principio factum est cum suis stellis, et terra cum animalibus suis, aqua quoque cum natatilibus atque volucribus: et breviter, omnia in speciebus suis simul educta sunt, quæ per simplicem virtutem motus cœli, et per virtutem stellarum, educi non poterant sine alio motore, id est particulari agente univoco, utpote speciei ejusdem, sicut sunt homo, leo, equus, et consimilia, quæ præter virtutem cœli et elementorum, requirunt specialem motorem ad sui generationem. Sunt tamen quædam non habentia magnam diversitatem in partibus corporis, ut plantæ et animalia aliqua, præsertim quædam reptilia et aliqui pisces, quæ non oportuit primo fieri in propriis speciebus, sed tantum in rationibus suis causalibus, id est seminalibus suis virtutibus, quia ad horum productionem sufficit motus cœli atque stellarum ex materia diversimode commiscibili. Propter quod dicit Avicenna in libro de Diluviis, quod mures quandoque generantur ex terra, et serpentes ex capillis. Hæc Albertus.
paras.en: Looking, then, at these things, Augustine says that the works of the six days were made together, and distinctly. Whence Albert says in the book On the Coequals: Augustine in truth holds that all those things were created together in matter and form which nature cannot produce of itself by the motion of the higher bodies, namely the heavenly bodies, and by the mingling of the elements. And therefore heaven was made from the beginning with its stars, and the earth with its animals, the water too with the swimming things and the birds; and in short, all those things were brought forth together in their species which could not be brought forth by the simple power of the motion of heaven and by the power of the stars without another mover, that is, a particular univocal agent [one of the same species as what it brings forth], such as man, lion, horse and the like, which besides the power of heaven and of the elements require a special mover for their generation. Yet there are some things that have no great diversity in the parts of the body, such as plants and some animals, especially certain reptiles and some fishes, which did not need to be made first in their own species, but only in their causal reasons, that is, in their seminal powers [Augustine's *rationes causales* or *seminales*: powers set in creation from the start, from which things later come forth], because for their production the motion of heaven and of the stars suffices, out of matter that can be mixed in different ways. For which reason Avicenna says in the book On Floods that mice are sometimes generated from earth, and serpents from hairs. Thus far Albert.

paras.t: Denique, ut Thomas super secundum Sententiarum fatetur, Augustinus vult quasdam creaturas in ipso creationis principio, id est primo instanti, fuisse in propria natura distinctas per species suas, ut elementa et corpora cœlestia ac angelos. Alia vero in rationibus seminalibus tantum, ut animalia, plantas et hujusmodi, quæ omnia in naturis propriis sunt producta illo opere, quo Deus post sex dies illos naturam prius conditam administrat. De quo ait Salvator: Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor. Nec in distinctione rerum attendendum esse ordinem temporis, sed naturæ atque doctrinæ: naturæ, sicut sonus præcedit cantum, sicque quæ naturaliter sunt priora, prius facta scribuntur, quemadmodum terra priusquam animalia, et aqua priusquam pisces; ordine vero doctrinæ, sicut patet in docentibus geometriam. Quamvis enim partes figuræ sine ordine temporis figuram constituant, nihilo minus geometria docet constitutionem figuræ, lineam post lineam protrahendo. Et istud fuit exemplum Platonis, ut dicitur primo Cœli. Sic quoque secundum Augustinum, Moyses rudem instruens populum de mundi creatione, divisit per partes quæ facta sunt simul. Hæc Thomas.
paras.en: Lastly, as Thomas states on the second book of the Sentences, Augustine holds that some creatures were distinct in their own nature by their species in the very beginning of creation, that is, in the first instant, such as the elements, the heavenly bodies and the angels; but others only in their seminal reasons, such as animals, plants and the like, all of which were produced in their own natures by that work by which God, after those six days, administers the nature he formed before. Of this the Saviour says: [[John 5:17|My Father worketh until now; and I work|Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor]]. Nor, he holds, is the order of time to be looked to in the distinction of things, but the order of nature and of teaching: of nature, as sound precedes song, and so the things that are naturally prior are written to have been made first, as the earth before the animals and the water before the fishes; and the order of teaching, as is plain in those who teach geometry. For although the parts of a figure make up the figure without order of time, geometry nevertheless teaches the construction of the figure by drawing line after line. And this was Plato's example, as is said in the first book On the Heavens [Aristotle's *De caelo*]. So too, according to Augustine, Moses, instructing an unlettered people about the creation of the world, divided into parts the things that were made together. Thus far Thomas.

paras.t: Sed circa hæc oritur quæstio, quoniam verba horum doctorum videntur ab invicem discordare, ita quod opinionem Augustini contrarie recitant, ut apparet. Albertus etenim ait, quod secundum Augustinum terra facta est cum animalibus, et aqua cum piscibus, etc. Porro Thomas refert, quod secundum Augustinum, elementa et cœlestia corpora sanctique angeli simul producta sunt, animalia vero et plantæ postea. Et respondendum, quod Albertus loquitur de animalibus, piscibus ac avibus, primo et immediate a Deo productis: et illa simul esse producta cum terra et aqua, secundum Augustinum, ostenditur ex præhabitis Thomæ verbis. Nam ait terram præcedere animalia, et aquam pisces ordine naturæ, non temporis, quemadmodum sonus cantum. Rursus circa hoc quæritur, quot animalia et pisces ac volucres, secundum istam opinionem, fuerint simul cum terra et aqua tunc facta. Ad quod pro nunc breviter dici potest, quod in qualibet specie duo individua, loquendo de his quæ ex commixtione maris ac feminæ naturaliter producuntur.
paras.en: But a question arises about these things, since the words of these doctors seem to disagree with one another, so that they report Augustine's opinion in contrary ways, as appears. For Albert says that according to Augustine the earth was made with the animals and the water with the fishes, etc. But Thomas relates that according to Augustine the elements, the heavenly bodies and the holy angels were produced together, but the animals and plants afterwards. The answer is that Albert speaks of the animals, fishes and birds produced first and immediately by God; and that these were produced together with the earth and the water, according to Augustine, is shown from the words of Thomas given above. For he says that the earth precedes the animals, and the water the fishes, in the order of nature, not of time, as sound precedes song. Again, it is asked about this how many animals and fishes and birds, according to this opinion, were then made together with the earth and the water. To which for now it can briefly be said: two individuals in each species, speaking of those that are naturally produced from the union of male and female.

paras.t: Præterea, quia nunc dictum est, quod secundum Augustinum omnia opera sex dierum sunt simul producta: quærendum, quid Augustinus ad litteram intelligat per cœlum et terram, quum dicitur, In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram. Ad quod concorditer dicunt expositores, et super secundum Sententiarum doctores, quod per cœlum intelligit naturam angelicam seu angelos; per terram vero, materiam prorsus informem omnium corporalium rerum, tam elementorum quam cœlestium corporum ac mixtorum, utpote materiam primam, ab omni forma per intellectum abstractam, quam dicit corporalia præcessisse ordine naturæ, non temporis, quia materia non potest realiter stare nuda, id est, ab omni forma substantiali abstracta. Per cœlum vero, intelligit naturam angelicam ut informem, seu in se consideratam. Cujus tamen informitas non præcessit tempore formationem ejus per dona gratuita, secundum Augustini doctrinam, qui dicit quod Deus fuit in angelis, simul condens naturam, et largiens gratiam. Quod autem ista sint de mente Augustini, patet aperte ex verbis ipsius super Genesim ad litteram, et in libris Confessionum, atque in libro de Civitate Dei, et infra tangetur.
paras.en: Moreover, since it has now been said that according to Augustine all the works of the six days were produced together, we must ask what Augustine understands literally by [[1:1|heaven, and earth|cœlum et terram]] when it is said: [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]]. To this the expositors, and the doctors on the second book of the Sentences, say with one accord that by *heaven* he understands the angelic nature, or the angels; but by *earth*, the wholly formless matter of all bodily things, of the elements as well as of the heavenly bodies and of mixed bodies: namely prime matter, abstracted by the intellect from every form, which he says preceded bodily things in the order of nature, not of time, because matter cannot really stand bare, that is, stripped of every substantial form [that is, prime matter never exists without some form; it comes first only in the order of nature]. By *heaven*, again, he understands the angelic nature as unformed, or considered in itself. Yet its formlessness did not precede in time its formation by the gifts of grace, according to the teaching of Augustine, who says that God was in the angels at once establishing their nature and bestowing grace. That these things are Augustine's mind is plain from his own words on Genesis to the letter, and in the books of the Confessions, and in the book of the City of God, and it will be touched on below.

1.title: Expositio litteræ, in qua describitur opus secundæ diei.
1.title_en: Exposition of the text in which the work of the second day is described.

paras.t: DESCRIPTA distinctione lucis a tenebris, modo describitur distinctio cœlestium corporum ab invicem. Dixit quoque Deus : Fiat firmamentum in medio aquarum, et dividat aquas ab aquis. Qualiter intelligenda sint verba hæc, Dixit Deus, Fiat, expositum est præcedenti articulo. Quid vero intelligendum sit nomine firmamenti, constat ex eo quod paulo post stellæ dicuntur positæ in firmamento. Itaque Deo dicente seu præcipiente, factum est firmamentum, id est cœlum stellatum, quod est sphæra octava, quia sub ea sunt septem sphæræ seu orbes ac cœli planetarum. Et factum est firmamentum hoc in medio aquarum ad dividendum aquas ab aquis. Et sumitur nunc firmamentum, prout includit septem sphæras præfatas.
paras.en: Having described the distinction of light from darkness, he now describes the distinction of the heavenly bodies from one another. [[1:6|And God said: Let there be a firmament made amidst the waters: and let it divide the waters from the waters|Dixit quoque Deus : Fiat firmamentum in medio aquarum, et dividat aquas ab aquis]]. How these words, [[1:6|God said|Dixit Deus]], [[1:6|Let there be|Fiat]], are to be understood was explained in the preceding article. What is to be understood by the name of firmament is clear from the fact that a little later the stars are said to be set in the firmament. And so, God saying or commanding it, the firmament was made, that is, the starry heaven, which is the eighth sphere, since beneath it are the seven spheres, or orbs and heavens, of the planets. And this firmament was made in the midst of the waters, to divide the waters from the waters. And firmament is taken here as including the seven spheres aforesaid.

paras.t: Et fecit Deus firmamentum. Jam ante ostensum est, expositionem illorum esse rationabiliorem, et textui atque antiquis ac sanctis doctoribus consonantiorem, qui dicunt in principio corpora cœlestia ac elementa simul producta sub distinctis et propriis substantialibus formis. Ideo, firmamentum et orbes planetarum in principio sunt creata, quantum ad totam suam substantiam : verumtamen non in tanta perfectione, quantum ad accidentales proprietates, virtutes et qualitates, ut postea. Unde, quod firmamentum dicitur factum die secundo, intelligendum est non de productione suæ substantiæ, sed de quadam sui completione, qua factum est magis completum et vigorosum in qualitate et proprietate suæ substantiæ, et in virtute causali, ad influendum elementis ac mixtis ad quosdam generales effectus, ut præinducto dixi articulo. Quemadmodum enim in Scripturis novi ac veteris Testamenti cœli dicuntur perituri et corrumpendi, non utique quantum ad suam substantiam, substantialeque esse, sed quantum ad accidentales quasdam dispositiones, qualitates et actiones, ita firmamentum et stellæ ac luminaria facta dicuntur post primum diem. Denique in Scripturis consuetus est iste loquendi modus, ut dicatur res fieri, quando accidentale aliquid agitur circa ipsam sive in ea : sicut quum filii Israel leguntur sibi fecisse præputia, in quantum non præsciderunt sua præputia juxta legem. In ultima quoque Ezechielis visione multoties dicitur : Facietis vitulos sive agnos, hoc est, illa aut illa die offeretis tot agnos ac vitulos. Sic et Jacobus apostolus in sua ait Canonica : Ecce dicitis, faciemus ibi annum, etc. id est, per annum unum manebimus illo in loco, qui ignoratis quid erit in crastinum. Fecit itaque Deus firmamentum, perficiendo illud in soliditate et causalitate, qua influit ad inferiorum conservationem ac regimen ; quia (ut ait Philosophus) oportet hunc mundum inferiorem, esse contiguum lationibus seu motibus et influxionibus superiorum, videlicet cœlestium corporum, ut tota ejus virtus inde gubernetur.
paras.en: [[1:7|And God made a firmament|Et fecit Deus firmamentum]]. It has already been shown that the exposition of those is the more reasonable, and the more in keeping with the text and with the ancient and holy doctors, who say that in the beginning the heavenly bodies and the elements were produced together under distinct and proper substantial forms. Therefore the firmament and the orbs of the planets were created in the beginning as to their whole substance, yet not in such perfection, as to their accidental properties, powers and qualities, as afterwards. Hence, that the firmament is said to have been made on the second day is to be understood not of the production of its substance, but of a certain completion of it, by which it was made more complete and vigorous in the quality and property of its substance, and in causal power, so as to exert influence on the elements and on mixed bodies for certain general effects, as I said in the preceding article. For just as in the Scriptures of the New and Old Testament the heavens are said to be destined to perish and be corrupted[[Agg 2:7||]][[Agg 2:22||]][[Matt 24:29||]][[Matt 24:35||]], not indeed as to their substance and substantial being, but as to certain accidental dispositions, qualities and actions, so the firmament and the stars and lights are said to have been made after the first day. Moreover, this manner of speaking is customary in the Scriptures, that a thing is said to be made when something accidental is done about it or in it: as when the children of Israel are read to have [[1 Mach 1:16|made themselves prepuces|sibi fecisse præputia]], inasmuch as they did not cut off their foreskins according to the law. In the last vision of Ezechiel too it is said many times: You shall make calves or lambs[[Ezech 46:15||]], that is, on this or that day you shall offer so many lambs and calves [the Latin *facere*, "to make", stands here for "to offer"; the margin gives Ezech. xlvi, 15, where the Vulgate has *Faciet agnum*, "he shall offer (make) the lamb"]. So also the apostle James says in his Canonical Epistle: Behold, you say: [[Jas 4:13|there we will spend a year|faciemus ibi annum]] [literally "we will make a year there"], etc., that is, we will stay in that place for one year; you who [[Jas 4:14|know not what shall be on the morrow|ignoratis quid erit in crastinum]]. God, then, made the firmament by perfecting it in solidity and in causality, by which it exerts its influence for the preservation and governance of lower things; for (as the Philosopher says) this lower world must be contiguous to the courses, that is, the motions and influences, of the higher, namely of the heavenly bodies, so that all its power may be governed from there [Aristotle, *Meteorology* I, 2].

paras.t: Divisitque aquas quæ erant super firmamentum, ab his quæ erant sub firmamento. Quæ et quales sint aquæ super cœlum existentes, magna atque difficilis quæstio est, de qua infra plenius tangam. Nunc breviter dico, quod quidam per aquas illas intelligunt nonam sphæram, quæ cœlum crystallinum ac aqueum appellatur : non quod vere et univoce sit de natura aquæ elementaris, sed quia cum ea in diaphaneitate communicet : sicut et cœlum empyreum dicitur igneum, non quod in calore, sed quia in splendore cum visibili convenit igni. Alii dicunt firmamentum esse veraciter naturæ elementaris, et similiter aquas quæ super firmamentum esse scribuntur, de quibus opinionibus paulo post diffusius referetur. Porro, quod aquæ dicuntur fuisse sub firmamento, non est intelligendum quod erant immediate sub cœlo stellato, sed manebant sub orbe lunari, secundum positionem superius amplius approbatam. Aqua autem et aer et ignis erant confuse permixta usque ad infimam sphæram cœlestem, secundum sic sentientes. Et factum est ita actualiter et in re, sicut dixit, id est, intelligendo ac volendo præcepit Deus.
paras.en: And he [[1:7|divided the waters|Divisitque aquas]] [[1:7|that were above the firmament|quæ erant super firmamentum]], [[1:7|from those that were|ab his]] [[1:7|under the firmament|quæ erant sub firmamento]]. What the waters existing above the heaven are, and of what kind, is a great and difficult question, which I will touch on more fully below. For now I say briefly that some understand by those waters the ninth sphere, which is called the crystalline and watery heaven: not that it is truly and univocally of the nature of elemental water, but because it shares with water in transparency; just as the empyrean heaven too is called fiery, not because it agrees with visible fire in heat, but because it agrees with it in splendour. Others say that the firmament is truly of an elemental nature, and likewise the waters which are written to be above the firmament; of these opinions more will be related at length a little later. Further, that the waters are said to have been under the firmament is not to be understood as if they were immediately under the starry heaven; rather, they remained under the orb of the moon, according to the position approved more fully above. Water, air and fire were mixed together confusedly up to the lowest heavenly sphere, according to those who hold this view. [[1:7|And it was so|Et factum est ita]] in act and in reality, as he said, that is, as God, by understanding and willing, commanded.

paras.t: Vocavitque Deus firmamentum cœlum. Sphæra octava dicitur firmamentum, quia firmissimum medium est inter aquas præfatas. In sua quoque natura est firmum ac solidum, juxta illud Job : Tu forsitan cum Deo fabricatus es cœlos, qui solidissimi quasi ære fusi sunt. Est item impertransibilis terminus prædictarum aquarum inter quas dividit. Vocatur etiam cœlum, quoniam celat et tegit sensibilia ista, atque a nostro abscondit adspectu exsistentia per ipsum. Et factum est vespere et mane dies secundus. Hoc exponendum est, sicut præcedenti articulo est expositum.
paras.en: And [[1:8|God called the firmament, Heaven|Vocavitque Deus firmamentum cœlum]]. The eighth sphere is called the firmament because it is a most firm medium between the aforesaid waters. In its own nature too it is firm and solid, according to that of Job: [[Job 37:18|Thou perhaps hast made the heavens with him, which are most strong, as if they were of molten brass|Tu forsitan cum Deo fabricatus es cœlos, qui solidissimi quasi ære fusi sunt]]. It is likewise the impassable boundary of the aforesaid waters, between which it divides. It is called heaven too, because it hides and covers these things of sense, and conceals from our sight what lies beyond it [Denis derives *cœlum*, "heaven", from *celat*, "it hides"]. [[1:8|and the evening and morning were the second day|Et factum est vespere et mane dies secundus]]. This is to be explained as it was explained in the preceding article.

paras.t: Præterea juxta eos qui dicunt, materiam primo creatam sub sola corporeitatis forma, et de materia illa esse producta elementa atque cœlestia corpora, sic exponenda est littera ista : Dixit Deus : Fiat firmamentum in medio aquarum, id est, cœlum sidereum producatur de materia illa informi et communi, et subsistat in medio illius materiæ, quæ interdum designatur nomine aquæ, quandoque nomine terræ, aliquando appellatione abyssi, ut dictum est plenius. Sicque dividat aquas ab aquis, id est unam illius materiæ partem ab alia. Et fecit Deus firmamentum, divisitque aquas quæ erant super firmamentum : hoc est, præfatam partem illius materiæ, existentem in loco eminentiori firmamento, divisit ab his quæ erant sub firmamento. Nunc enim per firmamentum designantur etiam orbes septem planetarum, qui facti sunt cum firmamento die secundo : quo etiam die (secundum istam opinionem) factum est cœlum crystallinum de suprema parte ejusdem materiæ, quæ in superioribus partibus suis subtilior fuit. De parte vero materiæ quæ mansit sub orbe lunæ, facta sunt elementa secundum istos non hoc die, sed postea. Sicque hæc dicta sunt fieri, quoniam proprias formas substantiales specificas acceperunt a Deo hoc die aut postmodum.
paras.en: Moreover, according to those who say that matter was first created under the form of corporeity alone, and that the elements and the heavenly bodies were produced from that matter, this text is to be explained thus: [[1:6|God said: Let there be a firmament made amidst the waters|Dixit Deus : Fiat firmamentum in medio aquarum]], that is, let the starry heaven be produced from that formless and common matter, and let it stand in the midst of that matter which is sometimes designated by the name of water, sometimes by the name of earth, sometimes by the name of the deep, as was said more fully above. [[1:6|And let it divide the waters from the waters|Sicque dividat aquas ab aquis]], that is, one part of that matter from another. [[1:7|And God made a firmament, and divided the waters|Et fecit Deus firmamentum, divisitque aquas]] [[1:7|that were above the firmament|quæ erant super firmamentum]]: that is, the aforesaid part of that matter, which was in a place higher than the firmament, he divided [[1:7|from those that were|ab his quæ erant]] [[1:7|under the firmament|sub firmamento]]. For here the firmament designates also the orbs of the seven planets, which were made with the firmament on the second day; and on that day too (according to this opinion) the crystalline heaven was made out of the highest part of the same matter, which was subtler in its higher parts. But out of the part of the matter which remained under the orb of the moon the elements were made, according to these, not on this day but afterwards. And so these things are said to be made, because they received their proper specific substantial forms from God on this day or afterwards.

paras.t: Præterea, quod primo dicitur, Fiat firmamentum ; deinde, Fecit Deus firmamentum ; et tertio, Factum est firmamentum : nequaquam superflue positum est. Insuper patet, quod dies ista secunda habuit non vesperam tantum, sed etiam mane, quoniam nox diei alterius eam præcessit ; et idem dicendum est de diebus sequentibus.
paras.en: Further, that it is said first, [[1:6|Let there be a firmament made|Fiat firmamentum]]; then, [[1:7|God made a firmament|Fecit Deus firmamentum]]; and third, [[1:7|it was so|Factum est firmamentum]] [Denis gives this as *Factum est firmamentum*, "the firmament was made"], is by no means set down superfluously. It is plain moreover that this second day had not only an evening but also a morning, since the night of the other day went before it; and the same must be said of the days that follow.

paras.t: Circa hanc litteram quæritur primo, an corpora cœlestia sint naturæ elementaris. Et videtur quod imo, ex textu præsenti, quum firmamentum sit factum in medio aquarum. Unde videtur sola divisione ab eis differre, et iterum quoniam supra ipsum sunt aquæ. Hanc quæstionem doctores super secundum Sententiarum satis discutiunt, et communiter Aristotelem assequuntur, dicentes quod sint alterius naturæ quam elementa.
paras.en: On this text it is asked first whether the heavenly bodies are of an elemental nature. And it seems that they are, from the present text, since the firmament was made [[1:6|amidst the waters|in medio aquarum]]; so that it seems to differ from them only by being divided from them; and again, because there are waters above it. The doctors on the second book of the Sentences discuss this question well enough, and commonly follow Aristotle, saying that the heavenly bodies are of another nature than the elements.

paras.t: Denique specialis est quæstio, an saltem cœlum crystallinum seu aqueum, designatum per aquas quæ supra firmamentum consistunt, sit vere de natura et specie aquæ. Et videtur quod imo, quia scriptura ista apertissime dicit quod supra firmamentum sint aquæ, et sub eodem contextu utitur nomine aquæ, ita quod videtur de aqua univoce loqui. Hoc quoque videntur prætendere manifeste alia loca Scripturæ veteris Testamenti, ut quum fertur in Psalmo : Qui extendis cœlum sicut pellem, et tegis aquis superiora ejus. Itemque : Laudate eum cœli cœlorum, et aquæ quæ super cœlos sunt, laudent nomen Domini. Et rursus in trium cantico Puerorum : Benedicite aquæ omnes quæ super cœlos sunt, Domino. Quum igitur magis debeamus sequi auctoritatem Scripturæ divinæ, quam dictamen rationis humanæ : videtur absolute dicendum, quod super cœlos sunt vere ac proprie aquæ, et quod cœlum crystallinum sit de natura aquæ : firmamentum quoque sit elementaris naturæ, videlicet igneæ, ut aliqui dicunt : vel partim igneæ, quantum ad stellas ; partimque aqueæ, utpote quantum ad reliquas ejus partes. Denique antiqui et sancti doctores, Augustinus, Basilius, Gregorius, Ambrosius, ita senserunt : quos Beda, Strabus, Damascenus, Magister Sententiarum, auctor Scholasticæ historiæ, Glossa, et alii multi secuti sunt.
paras.en: There is, further, a particular question: whether at least the crystalline or watery heaven, designated by the waters which stand above the firmament, is truly of the nature and species of water. And it seems that it is, because this scripture says most plainly that there are waters above the firmament, and in the same context uses the name of water, so that it seems to speak of water univocally. Other places of the Scripture of the Old Testament also seem plainly to point to this, as when it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 103:2|Who stretchest out the heaven like a pavilion|Qui extendis cœlum sicut pellem]]: [[Ps 103:3|Who coverest the higher rooms thereof with water|et tegis aquis superiora ejus]]. And again: [[Ps 148:4|Praise him, ye heavens of heavens: and let all the waters that are above the heavens|Laudate eum cœli cœlorum, et aquæ quæ super cœlos sunt]] [[Ps 148:5|Praise the name of the Lord|laudent nomen Domini]]. And again in the canticle of the three Children: [[Dan 3:60|O all ye waters that are above the heavens, bless the Lord|Benedicite aquæ omnes quæ super cœlos sunt, Domino]]. Since, then, we ought rather to follow the authority of divine Scripture than the dictate of human reason, it seems that we must say absolutely that above the heavens there are truly and properly waters, and that the crystalline heaven is of the nature of water; and that the firmament too is of an elemental nature, namely fiery, as some say; or partly fiery, as to the stars, and partly watery, as to its other parts. Indeed the ancient and holy doctors, Augustine, Basil, Gregory and Ambrose, held this; and Bede, Strabo, Damascene, the Master of the Sentences, the author of the Scholastic History, the Gloss and many others have followed them.

paras.t: Circa hujus quæstionis decisionem scribit Bonaventura super secundum : In hac quæstione, propter diversitatem positionum et debilitatem rationum, vix certum aliquid dici potest. Deinde post multa verba declinat ad hoc, quod per aquas quæ super cœlos sunt, intelligatur nona sphæra, quæ dicitur cœlum crystallinum, non propter veritatem naturæ aquæ, sed propter similitudinem in diaphaneitate, qua aqua non solum est luminis receptiva, sed etiam aliqualiter retentiva, ut patet in quibusdam lapidibus, qui non videntur de nocte nisi ponantur in aqua. Deinde, quasi concordando theologos atque philosophos, dicit quod Augustinus et alii Sancti dixerunt firmamentum esse de natura ignis, non quod habeat formam substantialem et speciem specialissimam ignis, sed quia participat lucis naturam secundum analogiam. Et quamvis istud sit bene dictum, quantum ad hoc quod videtur verba sanctorum theologorum pie salvare, et quantum ad homines concordare ; verumtamen si quis plenius curiosiusque voluerit informari, inveniet quod secundum intentionem et mentem Patrum jam præfatorum, cœlum crystallinum sit vere de natura aquæ atque formaliter frigidum, præsertim quum ponant aquas super firmamentum, ad temperandum solis et aliorum cœlestium corporum calorem. Unde Saturnum affirmant ceteris planetis frigidiorem, quamvis eis velocius moveatur, utpote altius situs propter propinquitatem suam ad aquas illas.
paras.en: On the settling of this question Bonaventure writes on the second book: In this question, because of the diversity of positions and the weakness of the arguments, hardly anything certain can be said. Then, after many words, he inclines to this: that by the waters which are above the heavens is understood the ninth sphere, which is called the crystalline heaven, not because it truly has the nature of water, but because of a likeness in transparency, by which water is not only receptive of light but also in some way retentive of it, as appears in certain stones which are not seen at night unless they are put in water. Then, as though reconciling the theologians and the philosophers, he says that Augustine and the other Saints said that the firmament is of the nature of fire, not that it has the substantial form and the most specific species of fire [that is, the lowest species, which makes a thing exactly what it is], but because it shares in the nature of light by analogy. And although this is well said, so far as it seems piously to save the words of the holy theologians and to bring men into agreement; yet if anyone wishes to be more fully and more carefully informed, he will find that according to the intention and mind of the Fathers already named, the crystalline heaven is truly of the nature of water and formally cold, especially since they place waters above the firmament to temper the heat of the sun and of the other heavenly bodies. Hence they affirm that Saturn is colder than the other planets, although it moves faster than they, being placed higher, because of its nearness to those waters.

paras.t: Hinc Thomas scribit super secundum : Circa hanc quæstionem fuit philosophorum diversa positio. Omnes enim ante Aristotelem dixerunt cœlum esse de natura elementorum : quod Aristoteles primitus improbavit, ponens cœlum esse sine gravitate et levitate aliisque contrariis, ut patet primo Cœli et mundi. Et propter efficaciam rationum ejus, posteriores philosophi, scilicet Peripatetici, consenserunt ei : unde nunc omnes opinionem ejus sequuntur. Similiter expositores Scripturæ in hac diversitate fuerunt, secundum quod diversorum philosophorum doctrinis erant instructi. Basilius enim, Augustinus, ac plures Sanctorum, sequuntur in his quæ philosophiam concernunt, nec spectant ad fidem, opiniones Platonis : ideo ponunt cœlum esse naturæ elementaris. Dionysius autem fere ubique in talibus Aristotelem sequitur, ut patet diligenter inspicienti libros ipsius. In talibus ergo dicta Sanctorum non sunt majoris auctoritatis, quam philosophi quos sequuntur, nisi quod sunt ab omni infidelitatis suspicione immunia. Hæc Thomas. Dicta autem Alberti libro de Coæquævis, concordant dicta Bonaventuræ.
paras.en: Hence Thomas writes on the second book: On this question the philosophers held different positions. For all before Aristotle said that the heaven is of the nature of the elements; which Aristotle was the first to disprove, holding that the heaven is without heaviness and lightness and the other contraries, as appears in the first book On the Heavens and the World. And because of the force of his arguments the later philosophers, namely the Peripatetics, agreed with him, so that now all follow his opinion. The expositors of Scripture likewise differed on this, according as they had been instructed in the doctrines of different philosophers. For Basil, Augustine and many of the Saints follow the opinions of Plato in matters which concern philosophy and do not pertain to faith; and therefore they hold that the heaven is of an elemental nature. But Dionysius almost everywhere follows Aristotle in such matters, as is plain to anyone who looks carefully into his books. In such matters, then, the sayings of the Saints are of no greater authority than the philosophers whom they follow, except that they are free from all suspicion of unbelief. Thus far Thomas. And the sayings of Albert in the book On the Coevals agree with the sayings of Bonaventure [Albert's treatise *De quatuor coæquævis*, on the four things created together at the beginning].

paras.t: Denique Beda ait : Cœlum sidereum constat esse in medio aquarum, quod de aquis factum credi potest. Nam lapis crystallinus, qui est magnæ firmitatis et perspicuitatis, de aquis est factus. Et secundum eumdem Bedam, aquæ sunt super cœlum instar glaciei firmæ ac solidæ. Hæc et plura similia habentur in Glossa, et allegantur a Magistro in secundo Sententiarum. In Scholastica item historia dicitur : Fecit Deus in aquarum medio firmamentum, id est quandam exteriorem mundi superficiem, solidam ex aquis congelatis instar crystalli et lucidam, super quam sunt aquæ ad modum crystalli congelatæ, ne igne solvantur. Quibus consonare videtur quod Josephus ait : Secunda die Deus cœlum super omnia collocavit, illudque ab aliis distinguens, in se ipso constitutum esse præcepit, et ei crystallum circumfigens humidum et pluviale, ad utilitatem quæ fit ex imbribus terræ, congrue fabricatus est. Ecce quomodo eruditissimi ac ingeniosissimi viri, propter auctoritatem Scripturæ, postposita philosophorum peripateticorum doctrina, sentiunt cœlos, id est sidera, esse elementaris naturæ.
paras.en: Again, Bede says: It is agreed that the starry heaven is in the midst of the waters, and it may be believed that it was made of waters; for the crystal stone, which is of great firmness and transparency, is made of waters. And according to the same Bede, the waters are above the heaven like firm and solid ice. These things and many like them are found in the Gloss, and are cited by the Master in the second book of the Sentences. Likewise in the Scholastic History it is said: God made the firmament in the midst of the waters, that is, a certain outer surface of the world, solid, of waters congealed like crystal, and shining; above which are waters congealed in the manner of crystal, lest they be melted by fire. With these what Josephus says seems to agree: On the second day God placed the heaven above all things, and distinguishing it from the rest, commanded it to be established by itself; and he fittingly fashioned it, fixing round it a crystal moist and rainy, for the benefit that comes to the earth from showers. See how most learned and ingenious men, on account of the authority of Scripture, setting aside the doctrine of the Peripatetic philosophers, hold that the heavens, that is, the stars, are of an elemental nature.

paras.t: Porro, quam acriter scribat Ambrosius in suo Hexaemeron contra aliter opinantes, patet in libro illo. Arbitror ergo in hac materia sobrie esse loquendum. Rationes quoque Aristotelis, quibus probat cœlum esse alterius naturæ, non sunt demonstrativæ, sed solum probabiles. Nempe, quod arguit de specialitate motus cœlestium corporum, quod non moventur ad medium, nec a medio, sed circa medium, quid demonstrat, quum et ignis in propria sphæra circa medium seu circulariter moveatur ? Et si dicatur hoc esse per accidens, utpote virtute sphæræ superioris ipsum continentis, non tamen motus ille est igni violentus aut penitus innaturalis. Denique in generationibus mixtorum, elementa levia, scilicet ignis et aer, naturaliter moventur deorsum : qui motus est eis naturalis per respectum ad naturam universalem. Sic dici posset de motu cœlestium corporum, quæ etsi essent elementaris naturæ, non tamen sequeretur ea corruptibilia esse : quum nec ipsa elementa sint corruptibilia secundum se tota, et aliæ rationes incorruptibilitatis possent assignari in eis.
paras.en: Further, how sharply Ambrose writes in his Hexaemeron against those who think otherwise is plain in that book. I judge, therefore, that one must speak soberly in this matter. The arguments of Aristotle too, by which he proves that the heaven is of another nature, are not demonstrative but only probable. For what does his argument from the special character of the motion of the heavenly bodies demonstrate, namely that they are moved neither towards the centre nor away from the centre, but about the centre, since fire too is moved in its own sphere about the centre, that is, in a circle? And if it be said that this is accidental, namely by the power of the higher sphere which contains it, still that motion is not violent to fire [in the old physics, a violent motion is one forced on a body against its nature] nor wholly unnatural. Moreover, in the generation of mixed bodies the light elements, namely fire and air, are naturally moved downwards; and this motion is natural to them in respect of universal nature. So it could be said of the motion of the heavenly bodies; and even if they were of an elemental nature, it would not follow that they are corruptible, since not even the elements themselves are corruptible in their entirety, and other reasons for their incorruptibility could be assigned.

paras.t: Hinc Thomas super secundum, positionem Aristotelis vocat opinionem, atque in prima parte, quæstione 68, multum sobrie loquitur de ista materia, dicens : Si dicamus firmamentum esse cœlum sidereum, tunc aquæ quæ sunt supra firmamentum, possunt dici illius naturæ cujus est hoc cœlum. Unde qui dicunt cœlum esse de natura elementorum, dicere possunt aquas illas esse elementares. Qui autem asserunt cœlum esse specialis naturæ, dicunt has aquas non elementaris, sed cœlestis naturæ esse ; et qui ponunt aquas elementares supra cœlum, dicere possunt quod non sint graves, sed subtiles ; nec fluidæ, sed tanquam glacies firmæ ac duræ. Unde a quibusdam cœlum crystallinum vocantur. Hæc Thomas.
paras.en: Hence Thomas, on the second book, calls Aristotle's position an opinion; and in the First Part, question 68, he speaks very soberly of this matter, saying: If we say that the firmament is the starry heaven, then the waters which are above the firmament can be said to be of the same nature as this heaven. Hence those who say that the heaven is of the nature of the elements can say that those waters are elemental. But those who assert that the heaven is of a special nature say that these waters are not of an elemental but of a heavenly nature; and those who place elemental waters above the heaven can say that they are not heavy but subtle, nor fluid but firm and hard like ice. Hence by some they are called the crystalline heaven. Thus far Thomas.

paras.t: Amplius, sicut Bonaventura tangit super secundum. Hi dicunt quod Deus in ordine universi magis attendit commune bonum et finis utilitatem, quam formæ qualitatem aut bonum specialis naturæ. Ideo sicut in minori mundo Deus posuit cerebrum sursum ad temperandum cordis calorem, sic supra cœlum sidereum posuit aqueum cœlum ad ardorem ætheris refrigerandum. Atque per istud solvunt argumenta quæ contra hæc fieri solent. Ego in ista materia assertive nil dico. Neque intentio mea est, in hoc loco horum discussioni plene insistere. Sed propter sanctorum Patrum reverentiam tetigi ista. Hinc in discussione hujus materiæ ait Bonaventura : Hoc præcipue attendendum est, ne in incerta materia aliquid certitudinaliter asseratur. Melius enim est pie dubitare, quam temerarie aliquid definire.
paras.en: Further, as Bonaventure touches on in the second book, these say that God in the order of the universe looks more to the common good and the usefulness of the end than to the quality of the form or the good of a particular nature. Therefore, just as in the lesser world [that is, in man, the microcosm] God placed the brain above to temper the heat of the heart, so above the starry heaven he placed the watery heaven to cool the burning of the ether. And by this they answer the arguments commonly brought against these views. For my part I assert nothing in this matter. Nor is it my intention in this place to dwell fully on the discussion of these things; but I have touched on them out of reverence for the holy Fathers. Hence, in his discussion of this matter, Bonaventure says: This above all must be heeded, that nothing be asserted as certain in an uncertain matter. For it is better to doubt piously than to define anything rashly.

paras.t: Insuper quæritur, cur in descriptione operis secundæ diei non dicitur, Vidit Deus quod esset bonum, quemadmodum in descriptionibus operum aliorum dierum. Ad quod eleganter respondetur in Glossa his verbis : Notandum quod opera secundæ diei, secundum Hebræos, non dicuntur bona, quum bona sint sicut et cetera : quod fit propter binarium principem alteritatis, qui primus ab unitate discedit, et in figura bigamiæ ac multorum reprehensibilium ponitur. Unde animalia quæ bina introierunt in arcam, immunda fuerunt. Impar autem numerus mundus est. Hinc Magister in secundo testatur : Non est hic dictum, Vidit Deus quod esset bonum, eo quod binarius esset principium alteritatis et signum divisionis.
paras.en: It is asked further why in the description of the work of the second day it is not said, [[1:10|God saw that it was good|Vidit Deus quod esset bonum]], as in the descriptions of the works of the other days. To this an elegant answer is given in the Gloss in these words: It is to be noted that the works of the second day, according to the Hebrews, are not called good, though they are good like the rest. This is because of the number two, the beginning of otherness, which is the first to depart from unity, and is set down as a figure of bigamy and of many things worthy of blame. Hence the animals which went into the ark two by two were unclean[[Gen 7:2||]]; but the odd number is clean. Hence the Master testifies in the second book: It is not said here, [[1:10|God saw that it was good|Vidit Deus quod esset bonum]], because the number two is the beginning of otherness and the sign of division.

paras.t: Verumtamen quidam dicit, quod responsio ista videtur trufatica esse, quia in Evangelio binarius laudabilis ac mysticus designatur. Unde Christus misit discipulos suos binos ad prædicandum. Ad quod breviter respondendum, quod tam indecens reprobatio potius posset dici talis, qualem ipse reputat præfatam responsionem, quæ etiam ex verbis Augustini sumpta videtur, quam et doctores super secundum concorditer approbant, utpote Thomas, Albertus, ac alii. Unde et Bonaventura scribit ibidem : Quamvis binarius minus ab unitate recedit, primo tamen habet rationem recessus in se. Idcirco per ipsum intelligitur divisio et recessus ab unitate virtutis et perfectionis, magis quam per alios numeros. Argumentum quoque illius non valet. Quamvis enim binarius quandoque accipiatur in bono, quia in omni creato invenitur aliquid perfectionis, nihilo minus secundum considerationem prætactam in malo accipitur : quemadmodum per leonem quandoque intelligitur Christus, quandoque diabolus.
paras.en: Yet a certain writer says that this answer seems to be a trifling one [Latin *trufatica*; the editors gloss it *falsa*, "false", referring to Du Cange's Glossary under *trufa*], because in the Gospel the number two is presented as praiseworthy and mystical: so Christ sent his disciples two by two to preach[[Luke 10:1||]]. To this we must answer briefly that so unseemly a rejection could more fairly be called what he reckons the aforesaid answer to be; for that answer also seems to be taken from the words of Augustine, and the doctors on the second book approve it with one accord, namely Thomas, Albert and others. Hence Bonaventure too writes in the same place: Although the number two departs less from unity, yet it is the first to have in itself the character of departure. Therefore by it is understood division and departure from the unity of virtue and perfection, more than by the other numbers. His argument, too, is not valid. For although the number two is sometimes taken in a good sense, since in every created thing something of perfection is found, nevertheless, according to the consideration touched on above, it is taken in a bad sense: just as by the lion sometimes Christ is understood[[Apoc 5:5||]], sometimes the devil[[1 Pet 5:8||]].

paras.t: Nihilo minus est etiam alia ratio, cur in descriptione operis secundæ diei omittatur illud, Vidit Deus quod esset bonum : quia videlicet distinctio aquarum ab aquis secundo die incepta, tertio die completa est, quantum ad aquas elementares, quando in unum congregatæ sunt locum. Nec ad introducendum hanc rationem magis litteralem, oportuit allegare infidelem in Judæum Judæorum doctorem Rabbi Salomonem, quasi ille melius dixerit quam tot doctores catholici : quia et ipsi doctores catholici jam prælati, eamdem rationem assignant, quam et Magister in historiis tangit.
paras.en: There is, nevertheless, another reason why in the description of the work of the second day the words [[1:10|God saw that it was good|Vidit Deus quod esset bonum]] are left out: namely, that the distinction of waters from waters, begun on the second day, was completed on the third day as regards the elemental waters, when they were [[1:9|gathered together into one place|in unum congregatæ sunt locum]]. Nor, to bring in this more literal reason, was there any need to cite the unbelieving Jew, the doctor of the Jews, Rabbi Salomon [that is, Rashi], as though he had spoken better than so many Catholic doctors; for the Catholic doctors already named themselves give the same reason, which the Master also touches on in the Histories [Peter Comestor, the "Master of the Histories", in the *Scholastic History*].

paras.t: […]denter se habuit, ultra modum, id est valde et ultra solitum communemque ministrorum eventum, non tamen immoderate per culpæ excessum, quia juste sic accidit. Et habuit greges multos, ancillas et servos, camelos et asinos. Quocirca quæri potest, an Jacob usus sit prædicta industria circa oves et capras dumtaxat, an etiam circa ceterorum pecorum greges. Ad quod non videtur ex littera haberi certa et manifesta responsio; sed quoniam infra legitur Jacob eduxisse de Mesopotamia tantam multitudinem non solum ovium et caprarum, sed et vaccarum, asinorum et camelorum, videri potest alicui, quod etiam de illis sic fecerit.
paras.en: […] he fared abundantly, [[30:43|exceedingly|ultra modum]]: that is, greatly and beyond what is usual and the common lot of servants; yet not immoderately, through any excess of fault, for it came about justly. [[30:43|And he had many flocks, maid-servants and men-servants, camels and asses.|Et habuit greges multos, ancillas et servos, camelos et asinos.]] Here it may be asked whether Jacob used the device described above only with the sheep and goats, or with the flocks of the other animals as well. To this no certain and plain answer seems to be had from the letter; but since we read below that Jacob led out of Mesopotamia so great a multitude not only of sheep and goats but also of cows, asses and camels, it may seem to some that he did the same with these too.
